question: In the Media.net Software Development Engineer (new grad) technical interview, a "standard Media.net question" is reported: **both a sorted array and a binary search tree give O(log n) search, so why use a BST over a sorted array?** The candidate is expected to discuss insertion and deletion costs, tree balance, and may face hypotheticals such as "what if memory were infinite?".
lookingFor: Looking beyond search complexity to the full set of operations.
Understanding of balanced versus unbalanced trees.
Awareness of memory layout, cache behaviour and practical constraints.
Handling follow-up hypotheticals calmly with reasoning.
answer:
**Search alone is the same:** binary search on a sorted array is O(log n), and so is search in a **balanced** BST. The difference is in the other operations.

| Operation | Sorted array | Balanced BST | Unbalanced BST (worst) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Search | O(log n) | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Insert | O(n) (shift elements) | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Delete | O(n) (shift elements) | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Min / max | O(1) | O(log n) | O(n) |
| Sorted traversal | O(n) | O(n) in-order | O(n) |

**Why a BST:** the data changes. Finding the position in an array is cheap, but inserting means moving on average n/2 elements. A BST changes a few pointers after finding the place. It also supports ordered queries efficiently: successor, predecessor, range queries, floor and ceiling, while still being dynamic.

**Balance matters:** inserting already sorted data into a plain BST produces a linked-list shape and O(n) operations. Use a **self-balancing** tree (AVL, red-black as in `TreeMap` or `std::map`) to guarantee O(log n) height at the cost of more complex rotations and extra node metadata.

**When the sorted array wins:** the data is static or read-mostly (build once, search many times), because arrays have **better cache locality**, no per-node pointer overhead, and are simple. Rebuilding or batch inserting then re-sorting can also be fine. A B-tree combines both ideas and is what databases use for disk-based indexes.

**The "infinite memory" hypothetical:** extra memory does not remove the cost of shifting elements, because that is a **time** problem, not a space problem. You could leave gaps in the array (a "gapped array" or library sort idea) or use a hash table for O(1) lookup, but a hash table loses ordering, so range queries and sorted iteration become expensive. State the assumption and name the trade-off each time.

**Summary:** choose by workload: frequent inserts or deletes with ordered queries leads to a balanced BST; static data with mostly lookups leads to a sorted array; ordered, large and disk-resident data leads to a B-tree.
followUps: How does a red-black tree or AVL tree keep itself balanced?
How would you find the k-th smallest element in a BST?
Why do databases use B-trees instead of binary trees?
When would a hash map be better than both?
